Actors deploy smart selfish maneuvers, using diplomatic talks as pretexts while projecting blame and maintaining conflict friction for leverage.

Surface diplomacy hides hardline escalation games where neither actor is willing to make unforced concessions first.

It is heartbreaking to watch ordinary people bear the economic and security costs of this endless political posturing between powerful states.

Actual Article Body:
Intelbrief /  Dueling Perceptions Cloud Resolution of the U.S.-Iran Conflict

October 1, 2026

Bottom Line Up Front

A week of high-level diplomacy on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly (UNGA), including the first U.S.-Iran meeting since June, failed to alter the strategic dynamics of the conflict. U.S. President Donald Trump rejected an Iranian proposal to fully open the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, contingent on the lifting of the U.S. naval blockade, unfreezing of Iranian assets, and other sanctions relief. The proposal was the subject of discussion in New York between Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Araghchi remained in the U.S. beyond the UNGA meetings, hoping for a formal U.S. counteroffer, but he departed on Tuesday, empty-handed. Yet U.S. and Iranian officials indicate that further talks will be held in the coming weeks in hopes of achieving a diplomatic solution or, at least, heading off a return to combat. Appearing on the NBC “Meet the Press” program on Sunday, Araghchi stated: “We are fully prepared for the time for the war to be resumed … even if it comes to a doomsday war,” while insisting that “[a]t the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy.”

Araghchi was in New York not only for possible talks with U.S. officials but also to help Iran’s head of government, President Masoud Pezeshkian, deliver a fiery speech before UNGA and meet with major U.S. media outlets. In his speech and interviews, Pezeshkian sought to amplify the domestic U.S. unpopularity of the conflict, painting Iran and its population as victims of unprovoked aggression. He and Araghchi expressed that deep-seated Iranian distrust of Trump and his team compelled the regime to insist that U.S. implementation of its concessions precede any agreed halt to Iran’s attacks on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The two senior leaders stressed that — in June 2025 and February 2026 — fruitful U.S.-Iran nuclear discussions were derailed by U.S. military assaults on Iran. Iranian officials also note that it was President Trump, during his first term, who terminated the 2015 multilateral Iran nuclear agreement, under which the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) had judged that Tehran was complying.

Insulating themselves from hardline critics who argue Iran should not engage with the Trump team at all, Pezeshkian, Araghchi, and other government leaders argue that Iran has largely prevailed in the conflict and can bargain from a position of strength. Government leaders argue Iran can utilize its “escalation dominance” — the ability to act militarily with greater strategic effect than the U.S. — to achieve its core goals at the bargaining table. Iranian negotiators echo the threats issued by Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) leadership that, should the U.S. refuse to lift the naval blockade of Iranian ports very soon, Iran will devastate the global economy and world energy markets with missile and drone attacks on shipping and on Arab Gulf state energy infrastructure. Regime leaders across the political spectrum argue Iranian strategy has depleted world oil reserves and U.S. munitions, increased U.S. interest rates and inflation expectations, and dampened the prospects for Trump’s Republican allies to prevail in the looming midterm elections. Tehran insists Washington must move first to accommodate Iran’s demands, and that unless Iran is able to use the Strait of Hormuz, it will not allow any country to use the waterway. On Wednesday, shipping observers reported the IRGC might have fired on three tankers trying to transit the Strait, an indication that Iran is willing and able to escalate.
